headline: Carry out the signature a caller asked for, compare a name by its own matching rule, and answer a proof of possession with which check failed.
summary: Four places accepted something and then did something else. A signer descriptor with a misspelled field was signed under the default digest with nothing reported, so a caller who asked for SHA-384 got SHA-256. A distinguished name written into a field that takes a common name was certified as one common name holding the whole text. An attribute whose equality rule is case-exact was compared case-insensitively, so two distinct names compared as one. And an authorization gate asked a decoded extension for a key usage name that decoder never defines, which anything on the object prototype could answer. Each is refused or corrected at the one place every route passes through.

Security: A signature verdict is assembled through the continuation the toolkit captured when it loaded, so a `Promise.prototype.then` replaced afterwards cannot substitute the result the verdict rests on. `p.then(f)` reads `then` off the promise at the call, and these verbs each computed `valid` inside such a continuation from the one boolean a cryptographic verify resolved: measured, a replacement substituting `true` for a `false` fulfillment value turned a tampered CSR signature, a CRL held against a key that did not sign it, a proof of possession over the wrong bytes and an attribute certificate held against a key other than its issuer's all into passing verdicts, each with the replacement reaching exactly that one continuation. `pki.csr.verify`, `pki.crl.verify`, `pki.attrcert.verify`, `pki.relatedCert.verifyRequest`, `pki.possession.verifyRequest`, `pki.cmc.verify`, `pki.est` enrollment and the Sigstore signed-certificate-timestamp check now take theirs from the capture, which `pki.cms.verify`, `pki.path.validate`, `pki.webauthn.verify` and `pki.crmf.verifyPop` already did. An OCSP CertID digest is taken the same way, a substituted digest being able to match a certificate the response does not name.

An authorization gate can no longer be answered by the object prototype. `pki.possession.verifyRequest` and `pki.cms.verify` ask the decoded KeyUsage extension whether the certificate's key may make a signature, and one of the names they ask for is `contentCommitment`, the X.509 spelling of the `nonRepudiation` bit. The decoder emits the RFC 5280 sec. 4.2.1.3 names and never that one, and the record it returned inherited `Object.prototype`, so a value set there answered instead: a certificate confined to `cRLSign` went from unauthorized to authorized under a single assignment. The decoded record now inherits nothing, so a name the decoder does not define answers nothing, and the two gates ask only for names it does define.
Fixed: An S/MIME signer descriptor that carries its fields on a prototype is read the way a property read reads it. A method on the descriptor's class is not a field, which `pki.smime.sign` already held, and neither is a same-named value that method shadows: a class defining a `digestAlgorithm` method over a base class that holds a `digestAlgorithm` string sent the string through as the field while the readable value was the method, and signing failed as `cms/unsupported-algorithm` naming an undefined digest. Such a descriptor now signs under the digest it asked for, or the default where it asked for none.

A distinguished name is compared under the matching rule its own attribute carries. Every attribute value was compared case-insensitively, which is correct for every attribute RFC 5280 sec. 4.1.2.4 requires support for and wrong for the ones whose rule is case-exact: `challengePassword` (RFC 2985 sec. 5.4.1), `localKeyId` (sec. 5.5.2) and `role` (RFC 5755 sec. 4.4.5) are all resolvable by name, mintable through `pki.x509.parseDn`, and compared EQUAL for values differing only in case. Name chaining, revocation scope and name constraints all rest on that comparison. Everything else keeps the case-insensitive rule, so a conforming PKIX name compares exactly as before.
Changed: A signer descriptor is held to the fields the verb reads. `pki.cms.sign` and `pki.cms.countersign` refuse a field they do not recognize, which `pki.smime.sign` inherits by signing through them, and which `pki.pkcs12.build` already applied to the same descriptors. Previously `{ cert, key, digestAlgoritm: "sha384" }` was accepted and signed under SHA-256, so a caller who believed they had configured SHA-384 got the default with nothing reported, while the identical misspelling one argument along in `opts` was already a hard `cms/bad-input`. A signer takes `{ cert, key }` or, where the signer is a key the message itself identifies, `{ spki, keyIdentifier, key }`; a countersigner takes `{ cert, key }`. Either form takes `pss`, `digestAlgorithm` and `combinedRsaSig` beside it, and anything else raises `cms/bad-input` naming the field and the form it was held to.

A name field takes a common name, and a distinguished name written there is refused rather than certified whole. `subject: "CN=Example CA, O=Example"` produced one RDN whose commonName was that entire string, escaped comma and all: the subject read back as `CN=CN=Example CA\, O=Example`. The refusal is in the shared name encoder, so it covers `pki.x509.sign`, `pki.csr.sign`, `pki.crl.sign`, the CMP, CRMF, attribute-certificate and trust-anchor builders, and a `directoryName` in a GeneralName. A common name is unaffected wherever RFC 4514 sec. 3 reads no attribute type at its opening: one that contains an `=` further along, such as `Example CA (v=2)`; one whose numeric opening is not an object identifier, `attributeType` being `descr / numericoid` and a numericoid carrying at least one dot, so `1=1` is a common name while `2.5.4.3=Example CA` is a name; and one opening with whitespace, which the grammar admits at no position. Pass `pki.x509.parseDn(s).bytes` for a distinguished name, or `[{ commonName: s }]` to certify the text as one common name. OpenSSL refuses the same string for the same reason, and the message names both forms.

`pki.relatedCert.verifyRequest` returns a verdict object rather than a bare boolean: `{ valid, verified, signerMaySign, signatureAlgorithm }`, plus `code` and `reason` when it did not pass. Read `res.valid` where you read the boolean. A bare boolean could not say which check failed, and there are now two: `verified` is the proof's own signature, and `signerMaySign` is whether the related certificate's keyUsage authorizes that signature at all, which RFC 5280 sec. 4.2.1.3 decides. A key-establishment certificate still passes, because RFC 9763 sec. 3.1 has such a key sign once for proof of possession. `signatureAlgorithm` names the algorithm the proof was checked under, which the request does not carry.
Added: `pki.schema.c509.parse` reports `signatureValueMinimalWidth` on a type-3 certificate. A fixed-width `r || s` names no curve, so the same signature padded to a wider accepted width reconstructs byte-identical DER: 64, 96 and 132 are three spellings of one certificate, and a C509 byte string is therefore not a unique identifier for what it encodes. The field is the narrowest width that represents the value, so `signatureValueMinimalWidth === signatureValue.length` answers whether this encoding is the canonical one, and re-narrowing to it gives a key that is the same for every spelling. Nothing is refused, and a genuine P-384 or P-521 signature reports its own width.
